correctness.rationale: The branch polynomial in z=x⁵ has distinct nonzero roots exactly when a²≠4, so the smooth double cover has genus four. In (1+az+z²)³ the coefficients of z,z⁵ are 3a and of z²,z⁴ are 3(a²+1), which give the four stated matrix entries. The contributing determinant permutation is a four-cycle of negative sign, giving −81a²(a²+1)²=3a²(a²+1)² in F₇. Every exceptional fiber retains two arrows with disjoint sources and targets, so the rank is two and either convention for the semilinear double iterate gives zero. For r and jr the stated u,v,w are invariant, and adjoining x satisfying x²−ux+1 generates the original field, confirming the degree-two quotient description. Each involution has two fixed points and Riemann–Hurwitz gives genus two. The pullback–norm relations sum to [2] on the genus-four Jacobian, giving the prime-to-seven isogeny. Each exceptional factor has p-rank zero, and in height four symmetry and slope denominator divisibility force all slopes to be 1/2. Thus the characteristic-seven dichotomy follows geometrically; the finite-field census is not used to cover arbitrary parameters.

originality.rationale: The earlier October 26 indexed record states exactly the characteristic-seven Newton and a-number classification of the same smooth marked family and actually lists all four nonzero polynomial entries in the same basis. Its four-cycle gives the same normalized determinant by one signed product and hence the same double multiplicities. Its supersingularity proof is by point counts rather than quotient isogenies, but the classification is not a new theorem. The accessible primary Ohashi–Kudo paper had already supplied the equivalent family and the sparse Cartier pattern. No substantively different invariant remains in the frozen finding.
residual_risks: Formal publication priority and the exact relationship to other quotient normal forms were not adjudicated. Neither limits the demonstrated coverage of the frozen invariants by the October 26 indexed text.

value.rationale: The marked Newton classification is useful mathematically, but as a distinct contribution it is already known in the audited evidence. The only displayed extra invariant is the signed determinant of a previously explicit four-cycle, and the double zeros merely read its product. The genus-two argument gives a valid alternate explanation using the two reciprocal involutions, but the record establishes no further structural theorem or uncomputed invariant beyond this already settled family. No distinct valuable remainder is supported for repair.
